intro: Zero-knowledge, from Semaphore as the concrete entry point through to circuit auditing. The specialisation with the fewest competent people in it, which is exactly why it pays.

groups.title: Semaphore — intermediate
groups.note: Anonymous signalling as the way into ZK that produces working code in a week rather than a month.

items.t: Semaphore identities 101: building secure anonymous credentials from trapdoor and nullifier
items.d: Identity creation, commitment generation, and why two secrets rather than one. Ships with @semaphore-protocol/identity code.

items.t: Getting started with Semaphore groups: Merkle trees for scalable anonymous membership
items.d: Incremental trees, adding and removing members, and choosing depth — with the anonymity-set argument for why depth matters.

items.t: Anonymous signalling with Semaphore: from votes to endorsements in dApps
items.d: Generating and verifying proofs with scope and message, demonstrated on private polling.
Full-stack boilerplate: Hardhat, frontend SDK and on-chain verification, end to end.

items.t: Deep dive into Semaphore circuits: Groth16, Poseidon and proof generation
items.d: Membership, nullifier and message components, witness generation, and performance benchmarks you ran yourself.

items.t: Preventing double-signalling: nullifiers, scope and replay mitigation
items.d: How the nullifier hash is derived, what the on-chain check must enforce, and the edge cases that break it.

items.t: Scaling Semaphore to millions: Merkle forests, PIR and proof delegation
items.d: Where the naive design stops working, what each optimisation costs in gas, and which are production-ready.

groups.title: ZK security auditing
groups.note: Feeds the ZK specialisation in the Web3 Security tab. Circuit bugs are under-constrained systems, not wrong arithmetic — that framing is the article.

items.t: Under-constrained circuits: the bug class that has no Solidity equivalent
items.d: A circuit that proves something weaker than intended, reduced to a minimal reproduction in Circom.

items.t: Soundness versus completeness, for people who audit
items.d: What each failure lets an attacker do, stated as impact rather than as definition.

items.t: Trusted setup: what you are actually trusting
items.d: Ceremony structure, toxic waste, and what a compromised setup buys an attacker.

items.t: Auditing a ZK application end to end
items.d: Circuit, verifier contract and the glue between — with the seam between them as the most common finding.

items.t: zk.golf and the art of the minimal circuit
items.d: Code-golfing constraints as a way to learn what each one costs.

groups.title: Crossovers
groups.note: Where ZK meets your other specialisms. Small audiences, but almost no competition and very linkable.

items.t: ZK proofs for verified-yet-private sender reputation
items.d: The ZK half of the crossover piece written up in the Email tab: proving sender reputation without disclosing the sending history behind it.

items.t: ZK validity bridges: are they really trustless?
items.d: What a validity proof removes from a bridge's trust assumptions and what it quietly leaves behind.
Which schemes survive, which do not, and the migration nobody has planned.
